Lanner falcon (Falco biarmicus) hatchlings emerge from eggs that have been incubated for approximately 32.75 days [ab = approximately 32.75 days] at a constant temperature of 36 °C [T = 36 °C], a duration that aligns closely with incubation periods reported for other medium-sized falconiforms. The wet weight at birth in this species is typically around 31 grams [Wwb = around 31 grams], reflecting the modest size of the altricial neonate relative to the substantial energetic investment required for egg production. This initial mass is notably low compared to the fully developed adult body weights documented for the species, underscoring the dramatic growth phase that characterizes the nestling period. The initial wet weight of the freshly laid egg has been recorded at 48 grams [Ww0 = 48 grams], a value that accounts for the combined mass of the yolk, albumen, and calcareous shell, all of which provide the nutrients and physical protection necessary for successful embryonic development under the thermal regime typical of natural cliff-nesting sites.

Under the thermal conditions that correspond to the active metabolic and foraging periods of this diurnal raptor, typically encountered at an ambient temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C], the developmental timeline of the Lanner falcon proceeds through a predictable series of post-hatching milestones. The nestling period culminates in fledging, the critical achievement of sustained flight, which occurs at 41 days after hatching [tx = 41 days after hatching] at a temperature of 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This relatively rapid progression from a dependent chick to a volant juvenile is characteristic of many falcon species and is thought to be an adaptation that minimizes the period of vulnerability to nest predation. Following fledging, the young bird enters a sub-adult phase during which it acquires the hunting skills necessary for independence, though it may still receive occasional provisioning from the parents for several weeks before achieving full nutritional autonomy and commencing its own independent foraging period. These early developmental events, taking place during the warmer months when prey abundance is highest, allow the fledgling to accumulate sufficient foraging experience before the onset of winter.

The physiological maturation of the reproductive system occurs over a somewhat longer timeframe than the somatic growth required for flight. Field records and captive breeding observations indicate that puberty, defined as the attainment of sexual maturity with the capacity for gamete production, is reached at 123 days after hatching [tp = 123 days after hatching] under thermal conditions averaging 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This timing implies that young Lanner falcons are physiologically capable of breeding within their first calendar year, although actual reproductive activity is often deferred in wild populations due to the constraints of territory acquisition, pair formation, and the need to develop proficient hunting abilities. The delay between the maturation of the gonads and the onset of actual breeding effort is a common life-history pattern among long-lived raptors, where reproductive benefits must be weighed against the survival costs of early reproduction.

The age at first successful reproduction, representing the time since birth at which an individual produces its first brood, has been estimated at 730 days since birth [tR = 730 days since birth] for Lanner falcon populations studied under typical environmental conditions at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This two-year delay between birth and first breeding is consistent with the life-history strategy of a relatively long-lived apex predator that invests heavily in each reproductive attempt. The species exhibits marked sexual size dimorphism, a common trait among falcons, which is reflected in the ultimate wet weight attained by adults. Females reach a maximum adult body mass of approximately 740.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 740.5 grams], while males, which are typically more agile and faster in flight, achieve a substantially lower ultimate wet weight of approximately 510.5 grams [Wwi = approximately 510.5 grams]. This difference in body size is thought to reduce intraspecific competition for prey resources and may also play a role in courtship dynamics.

The maximum lifespan recorded for Lanner falcons in the wild, based on long-term banding studies and field observations, extends to approximately 24 years [am = approximately 24 years] under the thermal conditions typical of their active metabolic range at 40 °C [T = 40 °C]. This longevity positions the species among the longer-lived members of the genus Falco and is consistent with a slow-paced life-history strategy characterized by deferred reproduction and extended parental care. Regarding the species' maximum reproductive output, females typically produce a single clutch per breeding season, with a clutch size of approximately 3.75 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = approximately 3.75 eggs per clutch] under optimal conditions at a temperature of 40 °C. The frequency of nesting events is generally one clutch per year [F_R_i = one clutch per year], although replacement clutches may be laid if the first is lost early in incubation. This annual reproductive investment balances the high energetic demands of producing and incubating a clutch of relatively large eggs against the survival benefits of maintaining adult body condition for future breeding seasons, a trade-off that is central to the species' population dynamics in the variable Mediterranean and sub-Saharan environments it inhabits.
